Same USHMM page lists larger 1950 remnants in almost every other occupied country: Poland about 45,000, Hungary 190,000, Romania ~280,000, Soviet Union ~2 million, France 235,000, Germany 37,000, Italy 35,000, Austria 18,000 https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/remaining-jewish-population-of-europe-in-1945 . Czechoslovakia's 17,000 exceeds only the smallest communities like Greece 7,000, Yugoslavia 3,500, Bulgaria 6,500 https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/remaining-jewish-population-of-europe-in-1945 , not "most" occupied countries. This documents near-annihilation, not a relatively large remaining population.

Claim: Effective Altruism as a creed prescribes earning more money in order to give more to charity.

## Your earlier research
The claim is broadly accurate but oversimplified. Effective Altruism (EA) has no single binding 'creed'. It is a philosophy and community built on using evidence and reason to do the most good. 'Earning to give' is one recognized career path within EA. It was popularized by 80,000 Hours around 2011–2013, and William MacAskill and Peter Singer have both promoted it. It is not a universal prescription. From about 2015–2023, 80,000 Hours moved away from recommending earning to give as the default for most people. Instead it emphasized direct work in high-impact fields such as AI safety, biosecurity and policy. It said that only some people, whose skills fit, should pursue high-earning careers. The article interprets Yudkowsky's 'pivotal act' as terrorism anyone building AGI 'must do' to stop competition. Yudkowsky's own definition is narrower: 'We need to align the performance of some large task, a 'pivotal act' that prevents other people from building an unaligned AGI that destroys the world. While the number of actors with AGI is few or one, they must execute some "pivotal act", strong enough to flip the gameboard, using an AGI powerful enough to do that.' https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities

His stock example is '"burn all GPUs"' but he explicitly says 'This is not what I think you'd actually want to do' and 'I don't *actually* advocate doing that; it's just a mild overestimate for the rough power level of what you'd have to do, and the rough level of machine cognition required to do that, in order to prevent somebody else from destroying the world in six months or three years.' https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities

Summaries stress it is the first / whoever-builds-first actor using an aligned AGI to do it, not 'anyone making AGI' as a general human obligation: 'To avoid catastrophe, whoever builds AGI first will have to a) align it to some extent, and b) decide not to scale it up beyond the point where their alignment techniques fail, and c) do some pivotal act that prevents others from scaling it up to that level.' https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities and 'it may be necessary for the first lab that creates a sufficiently aligned AGI to perform a pivotal act to prevent the other labs from creating an unaligned AGI.' https://github.com/centresecuriteia/textbook/blob/main/docs/chapters/03/04.md

Motive is framed as preventing omnicide ('prevent Facebook AI Research from destroying the world six months later'), not commercial 'competition' https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uMQ3cqWDPHhjtiesc/agi-ruin-a-list-of-lethalities . Separately, in his 2023 Time op-ed Yudkowsky advocated state action under treaty — 'including an indefinite worldwide moratorium on large AI training runs' with participating countries willing to take military action, such as 'destroy[ing] a rogue datacenter by airstrike', to enforce such a moratorium https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliezer_Yudkowsky — i.e. government military/law-enforcement, not non-state 'terrorism' by AGI builders, and to be performed by/through AGI, not humans committing terrorist attacks.

He explicitly adds "This is not what I think you'd actually want to do" and "I don't *actually* advocate doing that; it's just a mild overestimate for the rough power level" https://intelligence.org/2022/06/10/agi-ruin/ . Secondary summaries confirm a pivotal act is "something you can get the aligned superintelligent AI to do to prevent any other labs from building unaligned AI" https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/pPPy5pAavWP8JpRnZ/is-ai-alignment-enough , e.g. "melting all GPUs" / "subtly change all GPUs globally so that they can no longer be used to create an AGI" https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/DdmA5ElRpRPE9ZHEk/crosspost-ai-regulation-may-be-more-important-than-ai-alignment-for-existential-safety , "Releasing nanomachines that hunt down and burn all GPUs" https://manifold.markets/XXX/is-there-a-pivotal-weak-act , and Yudkowsky "stressed he intended to define a pivotal act as an act that involves the use of powerful AI" https://stampy.ai/wiki/What_are_%22pivotal_acts%22%3F . Separately in 2023 Yudkowsky advocated state enforcement in TIME "Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough. We Need to Shut it All Down" https://time.com/6266923/ai-eliezer-yudkowsky-open-letter-not-enough/ : "If intelligence says that a country outside the agreement is building a GPU cluster, be less scared of a shooting conflict between nations than of the moratorium being violated; be willing to destroy a rogue datacenter by airstrike" https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/be-willing-to-destroy-a-rogue-data-center-by-airstrike-leading-ai-alignment-researcher-pens-time-piece-calling-for-ban-on-large-gpu-clusters/ and "Make it explicit... preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange" https://archerships.com/archerships-essays/don-t-let-the-yuddites-kill-you-and-your-loved-ones/ . Multi-agent/Ultra is described as a mode/feature of GPT-5.6/Sol, not as Terra/Luna themselves: "Multi-agent [beta]: lets a GPT-5.6 instance coordinate multiple subagents in parallel and synthesize their results. cascade.findings: Claim is well-supported by labor history sources and is not misleading. The AFL was founded in 1886 as a loose federation of craft unions under Samuel Gompers, dedicated to principles of craft unionism https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Its approximately 100 national and international unions retained full autonomy and each received "exclusive jurisdiction" over a craft, with "one union per craft; one craft per union," which produced bitter jurisdictional disputes between affiliates https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Craft unions are described as organizing by specific craft/trade (e.g., all carpenters in carpenters' union, plasterers in plasterers' union) with own administration, agreements and halls https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Coming out of guild tradition, they policed how work was done by "maintaining standards for admission into the trade; requiring entrants to go through an apprenticeship program controlled by the union, rather than the employer; and dictating the processes, tools, standards, and pace of work" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Related summaries note membership was exclusive to those with particular skills to maintain strong control over labor supply in specialized areas, limiting membership to skilled workers and excluding unskilled workers, with craft exclusivity creating barriers to entry https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . AFL unions required union members only via closed shop and "Selective admission to apprenticeships restricted membership, thereby artificially limiting the supply of skilled labor" is the standard textbook description of early trade-union control.

samples.research:
The claim is an author's rule of thumb. The pages below support only part of it, and I found no study that measures the dating-versus-effort relationship directly.

Support for rough proportionality in the number of asks: Large online-dating datasets show fairly stable average reply rates. In one site's data, men's first messages got a 7.5% reply rate and women's got 9.3% (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1401.5710). If each ask has a similar success chance, expected replies would rise roughly in proportion to the number of asks. That is a simple model, not a measured result.

Why it is not strictly linear or uniform:
- Success odds differ by who you approach. In an online-dating study, the probability of a reply falls as the recipient becomes more desirable than the sender. Men were more than twice as likely to get a reply from women less desirable than themselves, and the reply rate to more desirable women never rose above 21% (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aap9815). So a pool that is larger or more varied does not mean proportionally more dates.
- Replies depend on the other person's selectivity and how many requests they get. Women get far more first messages and so reply at lower rates, which the authors call likely a volume effect (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.01050). A study of speed-dating group sizes suggests diminishing returns for women as the pool grows (https://www.oii.ox.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Computational-Courtship-Dinh-et-al-25-Sept-2018.pdf).
- Many first messages go unanswered, with one cited study reporting 71% of men's and 56% of women's unanswered (https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/dating-in-the-digital-age/201710/online-dating-101-three-reasons-you-aren-t-getting-replies). Outcomes therefore vary a lot with the individual and the context.

Conclusion: Asking more people plausibly raises expected dates roughly in proportion. The claim that lowering standards and widening the pool scale linearly is presented as general fact without data, and the evidence suggests success rates vary with the person approached. It is overgeneralized and unsupported, so I rate it misleading.

cascade.findings: Claim is a rough heuristic with some basis but overstates linearity. In a simple constant-acceptance model, expected dates = attempts x acceptance rate, so asking out more people mechanically yields more dates and lowering standards raises acceptance rate — directionally true. Post claims Steam enforces its own DRM on all games, requires login every 30 days to reauthenticate, and games break 30 days after Steam goes down. This is misleading/false. GOG's own developer documentation confirms the GOG Galaxy client is optional and DRM-free, and single-player content works without any client or server connection (https://docs.gog.com/introduction/).

Did you know cornrows were used by runaway slaves to map escape routes, as well as store food for their journey

## Research findings

The claim that cornrows were used by runaway/enslaved people to map escape routes and store food is a widely circulated but unverified internet legend, not an established historical fact. Snopes investigated this story (originally in 2022 and again in 2026) and concluded: 'We read a number of accounts, and found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages' (https://www.snopes.com/news/2022/03/12/maps-cornrows-black-slaves-escape/, https://www.snopes.com/news/2026/05/16/slaves-braided-maps-cornrows/). Snopes notes the legend is mostly documented outside the U.S., tied to the story of Benkos Bioho/Biohó, who escaped slavery in 17th-century Colombia and allegedly 'came up with the idea to have women create maps and deliver messages through their cornrows' — but this is a specific South American folk legend, not a documented general practice among enslaved people in the American South. A folklorist interviewed by Snopes, Patricia Turner of UCLA, characterized these as 'kind of urban legends that serve a function of giving particulars to generalities' about real slave resilience, rather than verified historical events. Similarly, Truthorfiction.com notes the claim is 'not without folkloric precedent, bearing close resemblance to a similar story about coded quilts' whose own historical accuracy has been heavily disputed by scholars (https://www.truthorfiction.com/did-slaves-braid-routes-to-freedom-into-hairstyles/). On the food-storage claim, some sources reference Judith Carney's book 'Black Rice,' which discusses the possible African origins of rice and theorizes women may have hidden rice seeds in their hair — but a Lipstick Alley discussion including historical skeptics points out logistical problems: 'I'm just astonished that no one ever stopped and actually thought about how much rice it would actually take to feed a person vs what could possibly be put into hair' and that any grains 'would have sweated into mush and literally nothingness' (https://www.lipstickalley.com/threads/slaves-used-cornrows-to-transfer-and-create-maps-to-leave-plantations.4570251/). Overall, while the story carries symbolic and cultural resonance and is repeated across many blogs and even one small academic paper based on oral tour-guide accounts at Elmina Castle, mainstream fact-checkers have found no solid primary-source historical evidence confirming it as fact for American slavery, and it should be treated as an unverified legend rather than established history.

cascade.findings:
Post claims as fact that "cornrows were used by runaway slaves to map escape routes, as well as store food for their journey".

MAPS: The story is widely repeated as oral history/legend, most associated with Colombia, where "Benkos Bioho, a formerly enslaved man, escaped and built a Palenque village" and "Women in the community would use their cornrows to create 'maps' and pass on escape routes" https://caro.news/how-cornrows-may-have-helped-free-slaves-navigate . Summary of research notes: "Oral histories passed down through African and diasporic communities tell us that during the era of plantation slavery, cornrow patterns were used to communicate. Routes north. Directions to safe houses. There is no written colonial record of this and there would not be." https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean  and "The most documented example of cornrows used as communication comes from Colombia. Benkos Biohò was an enslaved king who escaped captivity and built San Basilio de Palenque, the oldest free African town in the Americas." https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean .

EVIDENCE GAP FOR U.S. / GENERIC CLAIM: "A Snopes investigation in 2022 found no documentary evidence for the practice specifically within the United States but historian Tiffany Gill noted clearly that the absence of documentation does not negate the oral histories." https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean . Similarly summarized as Snopes "found no tangible evidence of slaves in the U.S. actually using cornrows to convey messages." https://griffinsandgingersnaps.com/were-cornrows-used-by-enslaved-people-to-escape-slavery/ . Presentation as settled fact for generic "runaway slaves" therefore overstates documentation.

FOOD/SEEDS: The seed-hiding tradition has stronger academic support, but it refers to smuggling rice/seed for survival and transplanting African rice knowledge, not simply storing snacks for escape. "The tradition of hiding seeds in cornrows before boarding the ships is referenced by Professor Judith Carney in Black Rice (Harvard University Press, 2001) and her peer-reviewed article With Grains in Her Hair (Slavery & Abolition, 2004)." https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean . Also: "There are rice varieties still being grown today in Suriname, South America, in Maroon communities descended from people who escaped slavery... each variety carries the name of the woman who carried it to freedom in her cornrows when she fled" documented by researcher Tinde van Andel in peer-reviewed study in Slavery & Abolition in 2023 https://byot.substack.com/p/the-hairstyle-that-crossed-an-ocean . Related literature notes: "African women braided their hair and hid rice seeds as well as other grains in cornrows" and "Mothers often braided the rice into their children's hair to have something to survive on while on the slave trips or escaping" https://face2faceafrica.com/article/how-african-slaves-used-hair-to-smuggle-grains-into-the-caribbean-a-hidden-survival-story (via search snippet) .

Conclusion: maps-as-fact is legend/oral history without colonial documentary proof, best-tied to Colombia/Palenque not proven for U.S. runaways generally; seeds claim has oral-history + ethnobotanical support but post mischaracterizes it as generic food storage for runaway journeys.
